report:
What happened

On 18 June 2026, Saltbush Air flight SB512 was preparing to depart runway 09 at Tarlton Springs Aerodrome. The aircraft was a 50-seat twin-turboprop registered VH-SBQ. On board were 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew. The doors closed at 07:16 UTC, 40 minutes behind schedule, and the departure took place in the hour after last light. The aerodrome's only runway inspection that day had been carried out before the first scheduled arrival. It recorded the movement area as clear.

The tower cleared the aircraft for take-off at 07:29:10, with the wind from 090 at 6 kt. The tower did not offer a further runway inspection, and the crew did not request one. The first officer was flying. The take-off roll began at 07:30:02, with both engines set at almost identical power. At 07:30:29 the crew called V1 at 112 kt. Two seconds later the first officer saw two kangaroos crossing the runway from the northern side to the south, at an estimated range of around 200 m.

The take-off was rejected at 07:30:32 with the words "Stopping. I have control." At that moment the aircraft was travelling at 118 kt, which was 6 kt and 3 seconds past V1. It had 695 m of sealed runway remaining. The power levers reached flight idle within 0.6 seconds. One second later the No. 2 propeller and the right main landing gear struck both animals. Three No. 2 propeller blades were damaged beyond limits, and No. 2 reverse thrust was unavailable for the rest of the stop.

The response on the flight deck was prompt. Maximum braking was established 2 seconds after the decision, against a fleet average of 3.2 seconds, and No. 1 reverse thrust was selected at 07:30:36. Even so, the aircraft slowed less than the scheduled performance figures predicted. It left the end of the sealed runway at approximately 21 kt and ran onto the graded gravel of the runway end safety area, where its deceleration fell further. The aircraft came to rest at 07:30:57, 62 m into the 90 m safety area and 28 m short of its end. It was upright and on the extended centreline, and there was no fire.

At the pilot in command's request, the tower activated the aerodrome emergency plan at 07:32:10. No evacuation was commanded. Instead, the passengers left by the forward airstair in a precautionary disembarkation that began at 07:34:40, and all were clear by 07:38:48. Nobody was seriously injured, although one cabin crew member reported bruising during the disembarkation. The aircraft was substantially damaged, and both right main tyres deflated. Two kangaroos were killed, and the aerodrome was closed for 4 hours 20 minutes.

Why it happened

The occurrence began with two kangaroos entering the runway strip and moving onto the sealed surface. The investigation found it extremely likely that their presence influenced the occurrence. It led to two further events: the decision to reject the take-off 6 kt above V1, and the strike on the No. 2 propeller and right main landing gear.

It was extremely likely that rejecting the take-off above V1 contributed to the shortfall in deceleration. It was virtually certain that the strike also contributed. The strike damaged the No. 2 propeller, and No. 2 reverse thrust was then unavailable for the stop. Taken together, these left the aircraft slowing less than its scheduled accelerate-stop performance predicted. It was virtually certain that this shortfall in deceleration carried the aircraft past the end of the sealed runway and into the runway end safety area.

The rejection above V1 was shaped by the crew's training. Saltbush Air's rejected take-off training covered aircraft system failures below V1 only. It was likely that this influenced the decision to reject at 118 kt. This is a safety issue.

The animals were on the runway because of when the aircraft departed and the condition of the aerodrome's boundary. The departure took place in the hour after last light, which is the peak period of kangaroo movement. It was likely that this timing contributed. Repair of the perimeter fence had been deferred for three budget cycles, and it was very likely that this allowed the animals to reach the runway strip. This is a safety issue. Behind the deferral sat the regulatory framework. A documented wildlife plan was required only at aerodromes above a size threshold, and Tarlton Springs did not meet it. It was likely that this contributed to the fence deferral. This is a safety issue.

Nobody checked the runway before the aircraft lined up. No runway inspection was requested before this first departure after last light, and it was likely that this contributed to the animals being on the runway undetected. The arrangements for inspections explain why none was requested. A runway inspection was required only at listed aerodromes, and an aerodrome qualified for the list only after a strike had occurred. It was very likely that this criterion contributed to the absence of an inspection. This is a safety issue. It was likely that the absence of a documented wildlife plan also contributed to these inspection arrangements. The evening service itself had been approved as a schedule change, so the route risk assessment was not reopened. It was likely that this contributed to the inspection arrangements staying as they were. This is a safety issue.

The crew's response limited the outcome. Maximum braking and No. 1 reverse thrust were applied without delay, and it was very likely that this influenced where the aircraft came to rest, inside the runway end safety area.

One further matter could not be settled. The investigation examined whether the intensity of the runway edge lighting reduced the crew's ability to detect the animals, but it reached no finding either way. The lighting intensity was measured, but only seven days after the occurrence. Nothing showed how the lights were operating on the night, and the two accounts of the lighting disagreed. No study was found that links an edge light reading of 131% to the detection of an object on the runway surface. Resolving the matter would need evidence of the lighting on the night and of how that lighting affects detection.

What we found

A finding stated without a likelihood term was established as fact.

Contributing safety factors

  • It was virtually certain that a documented wildlife plan was required only above a size threshold that the aerodrome did not meet, and it was likely that this contributed to the occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • The perimeter fence repair had been deferred for three budget cycles, which was virtually certain, and this very likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • It was very likely that the departure took place in the hour after last light, the peak of kangaroo movement, and likely that this timing contributed to the occurrence.
  • With virtual certainty, the evening service was approved as a schedule change and the route risk assessment was not reopened, and it was likely that this contributed to the occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • A runway inspection was required only at listed aerodromes, and the listing criterion was a strike at that aerodrome. Both points were virtually certain, and this arrangement very likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • It was virtually certain that no runway inspection was requested before the first departure after last light, and it was likely that this contributed to the occurrence.
  • Two kangaroos entered the runway strip and moved onto the sealed surface, which was virtually certain, and their presence very likely contributed to the occurrence.
  • It was very likely that rejected take-off training covered aircraft system failures below V1 only, and likely that this contributed to the occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • With virtual certainty, the take-off was rejected 6 kt above V1, and this very likely contributed to the occurrence.
  • The No. 2 propeller and the right main gear struck two kangaroos, and this strike contributed to the occurrence.
  • Deceleration was achieved below the scheduled accelerate-stop performance, and this shortfall contributed to the occurrence.

Other factors that increased risk

  • It was virtually certain that the cabin floor proximity emergency lighting was partially unserviceable. It was very likely that this increased risk, although it did not influence this occurrence. (Safety issue)
  • The crew were operating the fifth sector, 11 hours into duty and 40 minutes behind schedule, which was virtually certain. It was likely that this increased risk, although the recorded data did not support any influence on this occurrence.

Other findings

  • A take-off commenced with a tailwind above limits was examined and ruled out as very unlikely, because the aerodrome observations and the recorded aircraft data both showed a headwind throughout the roll.
  • The investigation also examined a No. 2 engine power loss during the take-off roll and ruled it out as very unlikely, because both engines were at matched take-off power until the reject and the No. 2 damage began at the moment of impact.
  • Maximum braking and No. 1 reverse were applied without delay, and it was very likely that this reduced risk by bringing the aircraft to rest inside the runway end safety area.

What is being done

Aerodrome Standard AS-139 required a documented wildlife hazard management plan only above a size threshold, and Tarlton Springs did not meet it. No action has been recorded against this issue. [NOT ESTABLISHED: any response by the body responsible for AS-139]

The aerodrome's own works register recorded the northern perimeter fence as failed in 2023. Its repair was then deferred at three budget rounds. The investigation walked and photographed the failed section on 23 June 2026. Even so, no repair, funding decision or other response by the aerodrome operator has been recorded. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the aerodrome operator's response to the fence deferral]

The evening service had been approved as a schedule change, so the route risk assessment for Tarlton Springs was not reopened. On 19 June 2026 the Head of Flying Operations suspended the evening Tarlton Springs service. No review has been recorded, however, either of the route risk assessment or of the change process that approved the service. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the service will resume, and on what assessment]

Under the operator's procedures, an aerodrome could be listed for a pre-departure runway inspection only after a reported strike there. No provision asked crews to report sightings. The investigation raised this with the operator's Safety Department on 2 July 2026. The investigator considers that the issue warrants a recommendation in its own right. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the Safety Department's response]

Rejected take-off training covered aircraft system failures below V1 only. No crew had been given an obstruction on the runway as a training scenario. No action has been recorded against this issue. [NOT ESTABLISHED: any proposed change to the training syllabus or to the operations manual]

The cabin floor proximity emergency lighting was partially unserviceable because of a failed ballast, and the daily test could not detect this. The same ballast is fitted across the aircraft type, so the fleet-wide question is with engineering. This issue remains open until that answer is received. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the outcome of the fleet check, and any change to the 24-month test interval]

"the passengers left by the forward airstair in a precautionary disembarkation that began at 07:34:40, and all were clear by 07:38:48"CONTRADICTEDThe occurrence notification, a verbatim source, states: "passengers were disembarked by the forward airstair 4 minutes 8 seconds after the aircraft stopped". The aircraft stopped at 07:30:57, which puts disembarkation at about 07:35:05, not 07:38:48. The timeline entry (07:34:40 to 07:38:48, "Passengers clear 4 minutes 8 seconds after the aircraft stopped") contradicts itself on this point. The draft has taken the timeline's clock times, which conflict with the notification. The source conflict needs resolving before this sentence can stand.

recordCheck:
Mechanical record check

  • {"section":"What is being done","severity":"info","code":"notation-leak","message":"The text carries the outline's \"[NOT ESTABLISHED: ...]\" notation rather than saying so in prose (6 occurrences)."}
reviewNotes:
• [What happened] - Timeline entry 07:34:40 to 07:38:48 (precautionary disembarkation) says passengers were clear "4 minutes 8 seconds after the aircraft stopped". The aircraft stopped at 07:30:57, so 07:38:48 is 7 minutes 51 seconds after the stop. The figure of 4 minutes 8 seconds matches the length of the disembarkation itself (07:34:40 to 07:38:48), not the time since the aircraft stopped. The draft gives the start and end times and avoids the disputed phrase.
  • Timeline entry 17/06/2026 21:35:00 (daily movement area inspection): the stated source is the aerodrome daily inspection log, but the attached extract is annotated as the Tarlton Springs wildlife sighting log, 01/2025 to 06/2026. The supporting extract may be mis-linked. Separately, the log is dated 18/06/2026 while the entry is timed 17/06/2026 UTC. This may be a local-date versus UTC difference, but no zone correction is recorded.
  • Timeline entries 07:29:10 and 07:30:29: the tower passed the wind as 090 at 6 kt for runway 09, which gives a headwind component of 6 kt. V1 was calculated for a 5 kt headwind component. This may be deliberate factoring, but the basis is not recorded.
  • Causal chains: the edge "Maximum braking and No. 1 reverse applied without delay -> Runway overrun onto the runway end safety area" places a prompt mitigating action upstream of the critical event as a cause. Its direction and category may need review.
  • Critical event: the speed at departure from the sealed surface is recorded as "approximately 21 kt" in the critical event entry and as "21 kt" in the 07:30:51 timeline entry. The draft carries the approximate marking.
  • [Why it happened] - Positive event "Maximum braking and No. 1 reverse applied without delay": the causal link runs to "Runway overrun onto the runway end safety area", which reads as if the prompt braking led to the overrun. The draft treats it as limiting where the aircraft stopped. The investigator should confirm the intended direction of influence.
  • "Documented wildlife plan required only above a size threshold the aerodrome does not meet": this links to both the fence deferral and the inspection listing criterion. The draft attributes both effects at the single recorded confidence ("likely"), so the investigator may wish to confirm that this confidence applies to each link.
  • "Runway edge lighting intensity...": the note refers to "a 131% edge light" but does not say what the 131% is measured against. The draft reproduces the figure without interpreting it.
  • "Cabin floor proximity emergency lighting partially unserviceable" appears both as a safety issue and as an other risk factor, and it is not finalised. It is omitted from this section.
  • [What we found] - Excluded hypotheses (tailwind, No. 2 engine power loss) and the positive event: the findings outline gave no likelihood terms for these. Under the opening sentence, a finding with no term reads as established fact. That would overstate the recorded results, which are Existence Fail "very unlikely" for both hypotheses and Influence "very likely" for the positive event. I added those recorded terms. Please confirm or strike.
  • "Perimeter fence repair deferred for three budget cycles": the evidence entry places the fence pad "110 m before" the first carcass. The photograph entry and the kangaroo object give 138 m, which matches 1,188 m less 1,050 m. The significance line says "140 m apart".
  • Pilot in command duty start: the duty record gives sign-on at 06:30 local, and the captain's interview transcript says 06:30. The interview background states the duty "began 05:10 local".
  • Pilot in command most recent training: the crew records give the last cyclic simulator as 11/03/2026. The interview background gives "Recurrent simulator check, February 2026".
  • First officer time with the company: the crew records say 14 months. The interview background says 17 months (joined April 2025). From April 2025 to the occurrence is about 14 months.
  • "Fifth sector, 11 hours into duty": the "Evidence for influence" and "Evidence against influence" fields appear transposed or mislabelled. The "against" field opens with "For influence:" and contains both arguments.
  • "Departure in the hour after last light": the recorded existence term is "extremely likely". The findings outline narrows it to "very likely" as the findings scale requires. Likewise, the kangaroos' influence ("extremely likely") and the training's existence ("extremely likely") are narrowed to "very likely".
  • [What is being done] - "Perimeter fence repair deferred for three budget cycles", Evidence: places the fence pad 110 m before the first carcass. The "Significance" line in the same factor says 140 m, and the photograph note and the kangaroo factor both say 138 m. These distances are inconsistent with each other.
  • Investigation log entry of 2026-06-26: says the cabin emergency lighting functional check was raised off the first officer's interview account. However, the functional check record is dated 24/06/2026, which is two days before the interviews were completed.
  • Approved "What we found" section: some likelihoods differ from the recorded confidences.
  • It gives existence as "very likely" for the after-last-light departure and for the training factor. Both are recorded as "extremely likely".
  • It gives influence as "very likely" for the kangaroo incursion and for the reject above V1. Both are recorded as "extremely likely".
  • It omits the recorded likelihoods for the strike and deceleration factors, which are "virtually certain".
